Wikipedia’s Chinese painting article illustrates Huizong with Finches and bamboo
Met record: 竹禽圖 卷 (handscroll)

work.text: “At the back of a picture of some bamboos and birds painted by the Emperor Hui Tsung of the Sung dynasty, Chao Meng-fu … inscribed these words: What joy for trivial things to be limned by a hand that is divine!”
work.lead: Herbert Giles, translating an old record:

source.author: Herbert A. Giles
source.title: An Introduction to the History of Chinese Pictorial Art

work.text: His method in ink-paintings of bamboos was very tight and minute. He used one tone of dry ink without gradations (without notan, as the Japanese would say), getting the effect of density, where required, by letting less of the white ground show.
work.lead: Arthur Waley, quoting the Hua Shih Hui Yao:

source.author: Arthur Waley
source.title: An Introduction to the Study of Chinese Painting

moment.text: The emperor’s predilection for small pictures of birds and flowers became naturally a reason for an abundant production of similar things by the members of the Academy and also by later imitators.

source.author: Osvald Sirén
source.title: A History of Early Chinese Painting, vol. II

matters.text: Zhao Mengfu, whose praise of a Huizong bamboo-and-bird picture survives, was himself a descendant of the Song imperial family serving the Mongols: admiring the emperor’s brush was also remembering a fallen house.
